A canal about 227 kilometres long linking the White Sea with Lake Onega and the Baltic, dug in twenty months between 1931 and 1933 by prisoners of the Gulag, the Soviet labour camp system.

Stalin wanted it fast and cheap. Up to about 100,000 prisoners at a time worked through a northern winter with picks, shovels, wheelbarrows and wood, with almost no machines. Food depended on meeting quotas. Official records count over 12,000 deaths, and other estimates run much higher.

In 1933 a group of famous Soviet writers, led by Maxim Gorky, toured the canal and wrote a book praising forced labour as a way to remake criminals into good Soviet citizens. A brand of cigarettes was named after it.

The canal was a failure as a waterway. To save time it was dug too shallow for most seagoing ships, and it has carried little traffic. It became a symbol of the human cost of Stalin's first five year plans, alongside collectivisation and the Holodomor.
sum: A canal about 227 kilometres long linking the White Sea with Lake Onega and the Baltic, dug in twenty months between 1931 and 1933 by prisoners of the Gulag, the Soviet labour camp system.
